**Justice Connect — the charity that stopped explaining the work and showed it instead (2021–2024)**

People who need free legal help do not arrive saying "this is a tenancy matter". They arrive saying their landlord has stopped answering the phone and there is water coming through the ceiling. Justice Connect, an Australian legal charity, watched that gap swallow people: pick the wrong category on the intake form, or give up and choose "something else", and you land in the wrong queue or nowhere at all.

The fix was not a cleverer set of instructions. The charity gave the tool its own material — thousands of real requests for help, written in the words people actually used, each one marked up by a volunteer lawyer with what it turned out to be about. Working with the University of Melbourne, it had recruited 245 pro bono lawyers who between them added more than 90,000 of those notes to over 9,000 real samples by September 2021. In the year after the tool went live, Justice Connect reported that incomplete enquiries fell by almost half and service delivery rose 10%, and its paralegals said the cases arriving through the tool were easier to deal with.

Nothing there made the tool better at law in general. It got better at this charity's queue, on this charity's material, in the language its help-seekers really use.

You have the same lever on every prompt. Instead of "a client emailed me, unhappy about a delay", paste the thread. Instead of "make this paragraph better", paste the paragraph, name who reads it and say what it must achieve. Take one vague prompt of your own into this lesson's practice, hand over the real material, then run the new-hire test on it.

**World Health Organization — a health promoter, not a doctor (2024)**

In April 2024 the World Health Organization launched S.A.R.A.H. — Smart AI Resource Assistant for Health — a prototype it describes as a digital health promoter. It answers questions around the clock, in eight languages, on any device, about the conditions that shorten most lives: cancer, heart disease, lung disease and diabetes, along with quitting tobacco, eating well, moving more and managing stress.

The interesting part is everything WHO settled before a single question was asked. It gave the assistant a role — a health promoter, not a clinician — and a goal: help ordinary people take charge of their own health. It named the audience: the general public, anywhere, rather than doctors. And it drew a boundary in the same breath, stating plainly that the tool does not diagnose and does not give personalised medical advice. WHO asked for one more thing that specifications rarely mention: empathy, a real conversation rather than scripted replies.

The same underlying technology, briefed differently, would have become a symptom checker, or a research tool for specialists. It behaves like a health promoter because it was told to be one, and told what success would look like.

You are not launching a global service, and your version fits in one sentence at the top of a prompt: "You are an experienced [role]. Your goal is [what success looks like]. Write [the thing] for [audience]." Borrow WHO's last move as well — a short clause saying what the answer must not do. Then run a task you did last week with that opening line, and compare it with what you got without one.

**Wikipedia — the summary that was fluent and unusable (2025)**

In June 2025 the Wikimedia Foundation announced a two-week experiment: AI-written summaries sitting at the top of articles for readers on mobile, generated by an open-weight model, shown collapsed and flagged as unverified. The plan was put to the community of volunteer editors. Within about a day, after dozens of objections, it was paused.

The objections repay a close read, because they were not really about the technology. Wikipedia is the rare organisation that has written its definition of good down and made everyone work to it: every claim traceable to a cited source, neutral in tone, nothing added that isn't in the material. Editors ran the model over particular articles and found errors. Others argued the summaries flattened the nuance the articles existed to preserve — one wrote that readers would never get past the AI text to see what the article actually meant. The Foundation said people must stay central to deciding what appears on Wikipedia.

Notice that fluent was never the standard. Sourced, neutral and inside the material was the standard, and an answer that misses a standard is unusable however smoothly it reads.

You hold standards too, for length, tone and what belongs in — you have never had to write them down, because your colleagues absorbed them years ago. An AI has not. Before your next "summarise this", say the length, say the shape (five bullets then a one-line recommendation is a reliable default), say what to leave out, and add the sentence Wikipedia's editors were defending: use only what is in the document, and write "not stated" rather than filling the gap.

**BBC — teaching a tool the house style by showing it, not describing it (2025)**

The BBC funds the Local Democracy Reporting Service, whose reporters cover councils and courts for local outlets across the UK. Hundreds of those stories reach the BBC every day, written in the house style of the papers that produced them, and each one has to be reshaped before it can be published as a BBC story. In June 2025 the corporation began a six-week public pilot of Style Assist, an in-house tool that does that restyling — first with newsroom teams in Wales and the east of England.

What is being asked of it is worth noticing. The BBC's idea of "good" is not a paragraph of adjectives; it is decades of published stories that all sound the same way. The tool's job is to match that body of work, and to flag legal risks and missing attributions along the way. Rhodri Talfan Davies said that in line with the BBC's AI principles, nothing is published without being checked first by a BBC journalist — and during testing the tool sometimes muddled who had said what, which slowed editors down.

So: an existing standard, shown rather than explained, plus a human check on the details a copied style can quietly get wrong. That is the whole of this lesson, including its caution.

Your version is one email. Find a piece of your own writing that landed well, paste it in, and ask for the new one in the same voice, structure and length. For work you repeat — the weekly update, the client report, the lesson plan — write the headings out once and keep them to paste from. And add the line that keeps you out of the BBC's trouble: match the style, but take the content only from the new material.

**Government Digital Service — five short rounds instead of one big restart (2024)**

In January 2024 the team behind GOV.UK published what happened when they put an AI chat assistant in front of the public. The honest version: nearly 70% of testers found the answers useful and a little under 65% said they were satisfied — and that was not good enough. Accuracy, the team wrote, did not reach the level demanded by a site where being factually right is the whole job, and they had seen a handful of cases where the assistant stated incorrect information as fact.

Two tempting responses were available: ship it anyway, or scrap it. The team did neither. The experiment had run as five short phases of roughly a fortnight each, growing from about a dozen testers to a private pilot of 1,000, with something specific changed between rounds — including how much surrounding context was kept when long pages were handed to the model. They named the exact failures, changed those, and tested again. Later public pilots ran to more than 10,000 participants.

That is steering rather than restarting. Notice what came first: not a vague feeling that the thing was a bit off, but a written account of what was wrong and what better would look like.

Your version happens inside one conversation and takes seconds. When a draft comes back at seven out of ten, don't retype the brief from scratch and don't quietly settle for it. Say what is wrong and what you want instead — "half the length, and lead with the budget shortfall". Ask it to critique its own draft before you accept it. And when two specific steers haven't fixed the same problem, that is your signal to restate the whole brief fresh.
